title: Repositories and domain services
idea: A repository loads and saves whole aggregates as if they sat in a collection; a domain service holds a rule no single aggregate owns.
points: A repository exists per aggregate root and speaks domain words: `findById`, `save`, `overdueLoans`.
The interface lives in the domain; JDBC or in-memory adapters plug in outside.
A domain service is stateless and named for a domain verb, like `LendingService.lend`.
Application services only load, delegate and save; rules there have leaked.

hero.title: One lend request through the layers

steps.caption: The application service gets ids from the outside world, not objects.
It asks each repository for a whole aggregate by id. It never sees rows or SQL.
Lending touches a member and a copy, so one domain service coordinates both.
The service asks each aggregate to change itself. Each still guards its own invariant.
Back in the application service, both new versions are saved only if no rule failed.
The repository is an interface. Tests plug in the in-memory adapter; production plugs in JDBC.

code.title: The problem: rules in callers
code.caption: Two desks edit shared maps directly. The web desk lost the checks, so a copy is lent twice and a limit is broken.

walk.text: Raw maps stand in for storage, and every caller gets direct access to them.
The kiosk re-implements the two lending rules itself before writing.
Nothing forces the next caller to repeat those checks. Copy-paste drifts.
The web desk writes straight through: `C1` silently changes holder.
The output shows three loans for one member and a stolen copy.

code.title: The fix: repo + domain service
code.caption: Every lend goes through repositories and one domain service, so no caller can skip a rule.

walk.text: The repository port: collection-like, one per aggregate, no persistence words.
An in-memory adapter. A JDBC adapter would implement the same interface unchanged.
The domain service coordinates both aggregates, holds no state, and is where a two-aggregate rule lives.
Each aggregate still enforces its own invariant and returns a new version.
The application service loads, delegates, then saves both results together.
A broken rule throws before any save, so storage never holds half a loan.

pitfalls: A repository per table, such as `OrderLineRepository`, lets callers bypass the aggregate root.
Returning query builders or entity managers from repositories leaks persistence into the domain.
Putting every rule in a `*Service` leaves anaemic entities that are only getters and setters.

quiz.q: A rule says members under 16 may not borrow copies marked adults-only. Where does it belong?
options: In a domain service that sees member and copy
In the application service before calling the domain
In the controller that receives the HTTP request
quiz.why: The rule needs the member's age and the copy's rating, so neither aggregate owns it alone. A domain service keeps it in the domain, where every caller passes through.

takeaway: Repositories store whole aggregates; domain services hold rules that span them.
